acts.title: What an online community actually does
text: People with a rare illness can ___ support and advice from others in the same position.
Seeing and hearing each other online seems to ___ all the difference to how much people learn.
Anybody can ___ a course on one of these platforms, and most of them are free.
Members of a cosplay community often ___ part in conventions in the real world.
On StreetBank, neighbours ___ each other permission to borrow their tools.
The ultimate aim is that people ___ a better relationship with the street they live on.

items.q: Many of these communities cross international ___.
Education is a major reason for joining a ___ community.
Immigrants need to ___ to new things.
Living alone represents a dramatic cultural ___ for many countries.
The number of people living alone has increased ___ in recent years.
Older people spend ___ more time without their family than younger ones.
People who have a ___ illness can get support in online communities.
Cosplayers use these sites to organize ___.

tts: When we talk about communities, we usually imagine a group of people who live close to each other. However, the fastest-growing types of community these days are online.
Online or virtual communities get people with similar interests together, so that they can share those interests or help each other in different ways.

Many of these communities cross international borders. BookCrossing, where people leave books for others who enjoy the experience of reading with strangers, has members in a hundred and thirty-two different countries.
Virtual communities can just be for fun, but plenty of them have a serious purpose. Many people who have a relatively rare illness can now get support and advice from others with the same condition.

And education is a major reason for joining one. Massive open online courses are places where anyone can join an educational course over the internet. Distance learning is nothing new, but being able to talk and see each other online makes all the difference.

items.q: What is the talk mainly about?
o: Online communities and what people use them for

items.q: What does the speaker say about BookCrossing?
o: It has members in a hundred and thirty-two countries

items.q: What does the speaker say makes the difference to distance learning?
o: Being able to talk and see each other online

tts: People in an online community may simply communicate with each other online, but they may also meet up face to face in the real world. People interested in cosplay use online communities to organize conventions where everyone can get dressed up and meet other cosplayers.

And some online communities are more about improving the real community that you live in. StreetBank is an online community where real-life neighbours can offer to lend things like barbecue equipment, or offer to help each other out as they do up their houses or gardens.
The ultimate aim is to encourage neighbours to be friendlier and to know each other better.

items.s: Members of online communities never meet in person.
StreetBank is designed to connect people who already live near each other.
On StreetBank people lend each other equipment.
The stated aim of StreetBank is to make money for members.

tts: Emma lives completely alone on a remote Scottish island. Harry moved last year with his young family into the Lilac co-housing project in Yorkshire.
Emma: the first thing to say is that it is perfectly possible to live alone and be part of a close community. I am sure there are plenty of people in the Lilac community who live alone.
Harry: yes, absolutely. It can be a great way of having your own private space without being completely isolated. You know people are there if you need them.

Emma: not many people choose to live so completely alone, but I love it. I like people, and it is exciting for me coming here today and meeting so many new people, but I love the peace of being completely on my own. I live on a farm, so there are the animals, and if I really want to talk to somebody I do have a phone. Though I do not use it very much.
Harry: a lot of people in this country have a spare bedroom for guests. What a waste of space. When my brother and his family come to stay, we just book a guest room in the shared Common Hall.

items.s: Emma lives completely ___ on a Scottish island.
Harry says co-housing gives you your own ___ space.
Emma believes ___ of people in co-housing also live alone.
If she really wants to talk to somebody, she has a ___.
Harry thinks a ___ bedroom used twice a year is a waste of space.
Co-housing means having private space without being ___.

acts.title: The five verbs that carry half the language
rule: get, give, make, take and do carry an enormous number of common expressions, and which verb goes with which noun is almost never predictable from meaning. There is no rule to work out; there are patterns to notice. These are the ones that recur most.
points: Things you produce or bring about: a difference, a decision, an effort, progress, a mistake, friends, small talk.
Work, tasks and vague activity: a course, research, business, the washing-up, your best, something / nothing / anything.
Things you accept or occupy: part, responsibility, a decision (British), your time, a risk, notice, turns.
Things that come to you: support, permission, advice, an idea, in touch, married.
Things you hand over: permission, advice, support, a hand, an example, somebody a call.
eg: It makes all the difference.
make a difference — never do.
She made a decision, and then took responsibility for it.
make a decision, take responsibility.
They did a course together online.
do a course.
He did some research before he wrote it.
do research — never make.
Everyone can take part in a convention.
take part in.
We take turns clearing the stairwell.
take turns + -ing.
They get support and advice from others with the same condition.
get support.
Neighbours give each other permission to borrow things.
give permission — and you get permission.
Could you give me a hand with this?
give a hand.
I must get in touch with her.
get in touch with.
acts.careful: Support, advice and permission work both ways: you give them and the other person gets them. Choose the verb from the direction, not from the noun.

write.q: Write about 180 words on an online community you belong to, or one you have watched from the outside — a forum, a group chat, a course, a game. Say what people actually use it for and whether it makes any real difference. Use at least five collocations from this lesson, and underline them by writing them in CAPITALS.
plan: what it is and who is in it
write.model:
The one I belong to is a group of about four hundred people who DO A COURSE together every January and then never quite leave.

Most of what happens there is not the course. People GET SUPPORT with things the course has nothing to do with — job applications, a bad manager, a father who has stopped recognizing anybody. Nobody planned that.

What surprised me is how much of it runs on permission. Somebody asks whether it is all right to post something off-topic, forty people GIVE PERMISSION in the form of a single emoji, and the thing that actually mattered that week gets said.

Does it MAKE A DIFFERENCE? For the course itself, honestly, very little; I could have watched the videos alone. For the year afterwards, a great deal. About thirty of us TAKE PART every January now, and none of us needs the certificate.
